blocks.md: The Leibniz rule tells you how to differentiate an integral when the thing you are choosing appears in its limits, inside it, or both. Moving a limit adds or removes a sliver at the edge; changing the integrand shifts the whole area. In economics this comes up whenever a decision sets a cut-off — how much stock to order before demand is known, or the lowest wage offer worth accepting — and you need the first-order condition.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is how you optimise expected values when the choice variable determines what counts as a good or bad outcome.
Three effects: moving the upper limit, moving the lower limit, and changing the integrand itself.
Special case (fundamental theorem of calculus): $\dfrac{d}{dt}\int_a^t f(x)\,dx = f(t)$ — e.g. the density is the derivative of the CDF.
Order $q$ units at cost $c$, sell at price $p$, demand $D$ with CDF $F$. Expected profit:

blocks.tex: \pi(q) = p\left[\int_0^q x f(x)\,dx + q\big(1 - F(q)\big)\right] - cq

With $p = 10$, $c = 4$ and $D \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 100)$: $F(q^*) = 0.6$, so $q^* = 60$ and expected profit is 180 (a grid search agrees).

- Forgetting the boundary terms when the limits depend on $t$.
- Applying it when the integrand's partial derivative is not continuous.

- **Labor / search**: choosing a reservation wage or an education cutoff, where the choice variable sets an integration limit.
- **Micro / IO**: expected-profit maximization under uncertainty; auctions.
- **Econometrics**: differentiating expected log-likelihoods; deriving densities from CDFs.
